clinicalPearls: A congenital anomaly defined by an abnormally large optic disc, conventionally with a horizontal or vertical diameter of roughly 2.1 mm or more.
Two forms are described: a common form with generalised disc enlargement and a large but round cup, and a form with a superotemporal or inferonasal enlargement resembling a coloboma.
The enlarged cup produces a raised cup-to-disc ratio that can be mistaken for glaucomatous cupping.
The neuroretinal rim remains healthy and of normal colour, and the cup shape is typically round and central rather than notched.
Frequently bilateral and usually associated with normal or near-normal visual acuity.
May show an enlarged blind spot on perimetry but generally without progressive glaucomatous field loss.
Distinguished from glaucoma by a normal intraocular pressure, an intact rim, and a stable, non-progressive course.
Rarely associated with midline anomalies such as basal encephalocoele, so imaging is considered when other features are present.
reference.pathophysiology: Megalopapilla reflects a congenital enlargement of the scleral canal and optic nerve head, resulting in an abnormally large disc with a correspondingly large optic cup. The normal complement of retinal ganglion cell axons is distributed across a wider canal, so the cup-to-disc ratio increases while the neuroretinal rim tissue remains structurally and functionally intact. Because the enlargement is a primary developmental variant of canal size rather than a loss of axons, there is no progressive excavation or rim thinning as seen in glaucoma. The larger disc surface projects a correspondingly larger blind spot, but ganglion cell function and the visual field are otherwise typically preserved.
additionalInvestigations: Stereoscopic disc examination and disc photography to assess rim integrity
Optical coherence tomography of the disc and retinal nerve fibre layer
Intraocular pressure measurement to exclude glaucoma
Automated perimetry to document any enlarged blind spot and exclude glaucomatous loss
Measurement of disc diameter and cup-to-disc ratio
Neuroimaging when a basal encephalocoele or midline anomaly is suspected
redFlags: Progressive cup enlargement or neuroretinal rim thinning suggesting coexisting glaucoma
Raised intraocular pressure with a suspicious disc
Midline facial anomalies or features suggesting basal encephalocoele
Development of a glaucomatous or arcuate visual field defect over time
reference.prognosis: Megalopapilla is a stationary developmental variant with an excellent visual prognosis and normal acuity in most cases. Recognising it prevents overdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment for glaucoma.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the large physiological cup as glaucomatous cupping and starting pressure-lowering therapy unnecessarily.
Failing to appreciate that the neuroretinal rim is intact when interpreting a high cup-to-disc ratio.
Overlooking coexisting glaucoma in a large disc by assuming all cupping is congenital.
Neglecting to consider a midline encephalocoele in atypical or syndromic presentations.
references: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach
